A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Pref-CFR research. All pages, including v1 Appendix A and v2 Appendices A–D, support comparison. Retained equations, tables, and figures can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original Kuhn poker convergence experiments and two-player and three-player Texas Hold’em strategy and head-to-head results.

after.justification: v2 reports revised Kuhn poker experiments, additional Leduc poker experiments, and retained original Texas Hold’em results.

M1.justification: The preference-weighted RM/BR updates and vulnerability adjustment match between v1 Equations 10–13 and v2 Equations 13–16. However, v2 Section 4.1 excludes all-one preferences, which v1 permits as the original-CFR case, while v2 Appendix C still assigns unit preferences to unmodified information sets. Whether input handling changed or only its description is unclear.

E1.justification: v2 adds Leduc poker, using a 12-card, six-pair configuration with community-card play and two betting rounds. Kuhn poker and both Texas Hold’em settings remain. This extends coverage within the existing poker domain.

E2.justification: The new Leduc comparisons explicitly evaluate external-sampling MCCFR against Pref-ES-MCCFR in Figures 3–4. v1 contains no corresponding evaluated ES-MCCFR comparator. Comparator membership in the retained Kuhn and Texas Hold’em comparisons is unchanged.

E3.justification: Kuhn experiments change from a stated 10,000 iterations to reporting through 10^7 nodes touched. New Leduc experiments use external sampling and extend through 10^8 nodes touched. No conversion establishes equivalent budgets across versions. The six Kuhn preference configurations and Texas Hold’em settings remain.

E4.justification: Beyond retaining the Kuhn preference and RM/BR comparisons, v2 adds substantial Leduc sensitivity analyses. Figures 3–4 compare zero versus positive vulnerability, preference degrees 5 versus 10, and vulnerability values 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, and 0.50. These directly test vulnerability’s necessity and the trade-off between strategic style and exploitability.

E5.justification: The original-CFR Kuhn experiment changes from 100 trials in v1 Figure 3 to 30 in v2 Figure 1. The preference comparisons already used 30 trials. Both versions report 90% confidence intervals, and the Texas Hold’em table intervals remain unchanged.

E6.justification: v2 replaces the Kuhn trajectories under revised reported budgets and reports exploitability below 0.001 rather than below 0.01. It adds Leduc convergence and action-probability results, including higher exploitability with increasing vulnerability. These are not same-setting performance gains. Texas Hold’em Tables 2–3 and their reported strategy distributions remain unchanged.

T1.justification: v2 introduces an acceptable-strategy-space and style-distance formulation, Conjecture 3.1 on initialization-independent RM convergence, GWFP conditions, and a new Appendix D derivation identifying RM as a GWFP process. Existing Blackwell arguments largely move to Appendix B, with clearer distinctions between two-player zero-sum NE and multiplayer CCE guarantees.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains preference-controlled strategies with bounded performance sacrifice. v2 foregrounds CFR-comparable performance and potential insights beyond expert heuristics in the abstract and introduction, replaces the payoff-variability motivation with stronger emphasis on style and entertainment, and explicitly scopes the introduction’s NE guarantee to two-player zero-sum games.

C2.justification: The new motivation section substantially expands the mechanism explanation, including why aggregate style feedback aggravates reward sparsity and how iterative intervention could control convergence. Leduc results are interpreted as suggesting a unique NE and explaining the need for positive vulnerability. The existing limitation of manually configuring preferences remains.

D1.justification: v2 supplies a concrete repository hyperlink and extends the stated code release from Kuhn to Kuhn and Leduc. Appendix A adds Leduc rules and identifies the experimental 12-card configuration. Existing CPU, runtime, subgame-size, and leaf-estimation details remain; the Kuhn configurations are relocated to Appendix C.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Hannan, Shi and Littman, and Wakabayashi and Young, while removing citations including Berger and Farina et al. It adds a substantive connection to GWFP, but retains the principal positioning around equilibrium diversity and combining computational methods with broader equilibrium concepts.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and substantial explanatory passages are rewritten. v2 adds a dedicated motivation section, integrates related work into the introduction, and moves convergence proofs and Kuhn configurations into appendices. Broken appendix references and the stray drafting sentence in v1 Section 5.1 are corrected.

P2.justification: v2 changes the main text to a two-column layout, redraws Kuhn plots with nodes-touched axes and revised legends, and adds two Leduc figures. The two Texas Hold’em strategy figures are merged into one six-panel figure. Existing geometric diagrams move to the appendix, while the three table images are retained and resized.

improvement.justification: The Leduc sensitivity studies strengthen empirical support for the vulnerability mechanism, while clearer organization, repaired references, and a concrete code link improve usability. The gains are qualified: Figure 4’s caption contradicts its plotted call-probability trend, and Appendix D Equation 40 combines an averaged action value with an unnormalized cumulative payoff. The revision provides useful additional evidence without establishing a substantial overall increase in reliability.
